cards.title: AI Writes Slop Because It Doesn't Know Which Commodity Ideas You Agree With
cards.summary: Commodity content has value, and the differentiator is not a unique idea but which side of each settled debate your identity sits on, which AI cannot infer.
cards.use_when: Writing or briefing product-description and blog copy for a store, and AI output reads generic or off-brand and you're tempted to re-prompt rather than supply the missing perspective.
steps: Accept the source's framing: commodity content (e.g. 'save your coffee money and invest in the S&P 500' vs 'saving coffee money won't make you rich') is not unique to anyone and often the most helpful thing a beginner can read. It has value, just the lowest-leverage value.

For your niche (e.g. minimalist home goods, value-priced kitchen gear), list the recurring commodity statements the whole category makes. Example: cheap cookware ruins quickly, you must buy heavy pans, nonstick is bad.

For each, decide and record which you agree with and which you reject. That stance is the thing AI cannot supply and, per the source, is the reason AI produces generic copy: it doesn't know which perspective you hold.
Feed those recorded positions into the brief, not just the sales angle. Note in your brand's voice guide: never use the 'buy heavy pans' argument, we believe light pans used correctly outperform.
Keep a running log of the positions you've decided so editors and AI tools reuse the same ones rather than reverting to category consensus.
If you find a statement the whole category repeats and you genuinely can't pick a side, note it as deliberately neutral rather than letting the model default.
caveats: The source's coffee and S&P examples are illustrative, not research.
The source frames personality-first positions as higher-distribution, not guaranteed to convert; a product detail still has to be true.

cards.title: Write From 'I', Not 'You', to Escape Commodity Copy
cards.summary: Copy that addresses the reader with 'you should' defaults to generic advice; copy written from 'I think / I did' produces personality content that differentiates.
cards.use_when: Drafting product descriptions, founder notes, or landing page copy and the paragraph reads like generic category advice that any store could publish.
steps: Audit a draft and highlight every sentence that begins with or implies 'you should', 'you need to', or 'you must'.
Rewrite those as first-person experience, opinion, and observation: instead of 'You should test your products before launch,' write 'I tested this knife for a month before ordering 500 units.'

The source's operational rule is that 'you' framing is commodity (repeating what everyone says) and 'I' framing is personality content (what this particular person thinks about the world) which cannot be matched by category competitors.

Apply this to the store's operationally relevant copy: a checkout trust blurb, an about page, a product page note about a specific failure in sourcing or materials — these are the cheapest places to insert 'I' perspective.

Where a brand account rather than a founder is posting, keep the brand page to the agreed commodity ideas (e.g. '5 benefits of X') and reserve 'I' content for the founder's account — the source says brand content naturally underperforms human content.
Read the rewritten line aloud next to the original. If it would fit identically on a competitor's PDP, it's still commodity.
caveats: The source states 'you' content defaults to feeling patronizing in his experience; it's his stated framing, not a tested universal.
Personality content still has to be accurate about claims, shipping, and materials.

cards.title: AI Should Repeat You, Not Write For You
cards.summary: AI's leverage is in recombining your approved language into new mixes, not in generating net-new thinking from the same public dataset every competitor uses.
cards.use_when: Setting up a content production workflow for a store — delegating blog, email, or social output to AI and deciding which parts a human must do first.
steps: Draw the boundary explicitly. Human work: net-new thinking, first articulation of an idea, stance on commodity claims, and specific customer stories or founder history.
AI work: remixing sentences, passages and posts you already wrote into new combinations, cross-posting across channels, and templating.

Before automating anything, produce the source material. The source's ghostwriting analogy: a ghostwriter never invents the client's ideas, they stitch approved sentences from chapter one, two, three and four into something new. AI's capability is the mechanical version of the same task.
Build the library the AI reads from — wherever it lives (docs, a second-brain tool, a spreadsheet). The source's point is that the location does not matter, only that the AI can access it.

Example application: if you have five product-page paragraphs about your five material benefits, let AI create new combinations for category landing pages rather than asking it to invent material benefits.
As your library grows, ask what each AI-drafted piece added to the pool: net-new thinking or just another arrangement of what already exists.
caveats: The source argues the unautomated writing step is the highest-leverage thing you can do — this is a strong opinion, not a universal rule.
Merging prior paragraphs repeatedly can produce repetitive output; the source's use case is reposting and remixing existing high-performers across channels, not infinite novelty.

cards.title: Value Is Relative to Where Your Audience Is
cards.summary: Content value depends on the reader's stage, not the writer's, so advanced operators must deliberately decide whether to serve beginners with commodity content or serve peers with original thinking.
cards.use_when: Choosing what to publish for a store's blog or email list and deciding whether to write beginner 'how to choose' content or advanced, opinionated content for experienced customers.
steps: Identify where your audience actually sits. If most of your list is new to the category, basic guidance ('which size to pick') is not wasted — it may be the most useful thing you can publish even though it's written many times already.

Recognize the cost to you: the source says writing the same commodity idea a thousand times is boring and low-leverage for the writer, because you are not thinking anything new — you are repeating what you already know.

If you're burnt out on beginner content, that's a signal to add higher-leverage content — opinions, testing notes, failures — for the portion of your audience that has already graduated past the basics.
Segment or tag published content by stage so a newsletter to returning customers doesn't repeat the introductory piece they already read.

The source's utopian framing: let automation handle repeating the basics, and spend the human time on content that advances what you know. Don't conflate the automation of repetitive content with permission to skip thinking altogether.
caveats: There is no numeric stage band in the source; the beginner/advanced split is qualitative.
If you don't know your list's stage distribution, that's the missing input before deciding.

cards.title: Build the 'Unmade Data Set' From Your Own Stories
cards.summary: Since every competitor trains on the same public corpus, your proprietary history — mistakes, specific lived details, your path — is the only data no one else has.
cards.use_when: Filling out a brand/about page, a founder newsletter, or a retention email series and looking for content that differentiates rather than repeats category knowledge.
steps: Set aside a recurring block to write about how you became you as an operator: the mistakes you made running the store, the failed product line, the sourcing trip that went badly, the reason you started.
Pull the specific data points that only exist in your head. These are the 'unmade data set' — the source's term for content that cannot be scraped or generated because it's never been articulated.

Write them into whatever library your team and tools read from (docs, spreadsheet, second-brain tool like Obsidian) with a label so AI outputs can be instructed to include the ones you've already approved.

In copy, drop the story into the exact place the commodity version would go. The source's example: if the standard claim is 'we care about quality,' the differentiated version is the specific event that showed you why.

The source's counter to 'my life is boring': the mundane example was moving coast-to-coast twice in four years — he says at a dinner party someone else would immediately answer with their own version. Uniqueness is low but resonance is high.
Treat these as reusable: once you've written a story once or twice, hand it to AI to redeploy across channels instead of retelling it by hand.
caveats: The source says this is the highest-quality content he produces, in his own experience; it's not a measured ecommerce result.
Specific errors and failures have to be shared in a way that doesn't create liability or breach partner agreements.

cards.title: Personality Outperforms Credibility in Content
cards.summary: The source argues less-credentialed creators with strong personality content generally get more distribution than highly credentialed people producing flat commodity content.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much founder personality to expose versus how much 'expert' positioning to project on a store's about page, newsletter or founder-led social channel.
steps: Distinguish the two layers of association. Base layer: you write about the topic enough that people associate it with you. Second layer: the audience knows specific facts, perspectives and stories about you as a person.

Compare a generic cookware expert with no personal detail to one who mentions the chapter of life that pushed them to start, or the failed earlier attempt — the source claims the personality-heavy one typically outperforms.

Make it a light-touch practice: roughly the level of detail someone shares in a first coffee meeting — where you're from, what you're into, what you're working on. The source's framing is that writing online is the scalable version of the same conversation.

Apply per-channel: founder's account can carry the personality-heavy content; the brand's account repeats commodity positions without the personal detail — the source says branded content 'always underperforms' human content.
For a store, the practical use is in emails and product pages where a person is attached to the product (founder, buyer, quality lead) — sign the piece with the human, not the brand.
Optional brand-level version: profile a named staff member with a specific story connecting them to the product, so the store gets personality content it couldn't get from an anonymous account.
caveats: The source supports his claim mainly with the Ray Dalio-style comparison, where a less-credentialed personality creator out-distributes a heavily credentialed one — an illustration, not measurement.
Personality is not a substitute for accuracy. Statements about products, materials, sourcing still need to be true.

cards.title: Timely vs Timeless Content: Set Expectations Before You Publish
cards.summary: Every piece of content sits on a timely–timeless spectrum; timely content gives high 24-hour value and near-zero long-term value, and the reverse for timeless, so match expectations to the type.
cards.use_when: Planning a store's content calendar — deciding which launches, memes, or promotions to make and which should be evergreen pieces you re-use for years.
steps: Before making the piece, label it timely or timeless. Timely: reacts to an announcement, holiday, or trend; expected payoff is measured in hours or days.
Timeless: an essay, a thorough how-to, a story you'll reference for years. It's unrealistic to expect the same short-term spike as the timely piece.
If you want more compounding content, shift the mix toward timeless — the type you can pull quotes and paragraphs from indefinitely without rewriting.

Apply to store operations: a Black Friday countdown post is timely by design, so retire and archive it after the window rather than resurfacing it out of campaign. A 'how to choose your first [product]' piece is timeless and can be reposted or repurposed for a long time.

The source's specific example of the change: 'here is how to start a Substack' is timeless; 'Substack just launched this feature, here's how to start a Substack in 2026' is timely — the single date changes the whole value profile.
Decide which categories of piece belong to which bucket and schedule them separately, so the memory of a low-performing timely piece doesn't distort the plan for a timeless one.
caveats: The source describes a single long essay that kept paying off for a decade — a personal example, not a promise about distribution.
There is no numeric threshold for 'high' vs 'low' value in the source; it's a qualitative spectrum.

cards.title: Volume and Topic Concentration Create Association (Ownership Is Just Association)
cards.summary: You don't own words, ideas or phrases — you own the audience's association between a topic and you, and the simplest way to build it is to publish about a narrow set of topics repeatedly.
cards.use_when: Choosing what a store's content program should be known for, and deciding whether to write broadly or concentrate on a narrow set of positions to drive association with the category.
steps: Treat the source's framing: since language and most word pairings are open source, ownership is really association — you can achieve it in many ways, the easiest of which is volume on a topic.
Pick a small number of topics for the store (e.g. three or four category positions plus the store's particular angle) and publish consistently on those rather than spreading thin across everything.
Example of association by volume: writing constantly about AI startup ideas made people associate that topic with the source's podcast; repetition is what built the association, not any single piece.
For the store, this means a repeating format works: a regular series of posts on the same home-maintenance problem creates the mental link between store and problem over time.
Watch the counter-case: writing about everything, the source says, means you never go deep enough on one thing to establish the association.
Record your repeating formats as a reusable asset — the source calls this 'approved language' that once you've said the same thing well once or twice, AI can repeat it.
caveats: The source's caution is explicit: broad writing is the fastest way to have nothing associated with you.
Volume is a strategy the source states as 'the easiest way to achieve association' — he doesn't quantify how much.

cards.title: Voice Is Built From Identifiable Variables, Not Magic
cards.summary: Voice is a bundle of word choice, sentence length/structure and perspective-taking that can be identified and edited rather than treated as untouchable mystique.
cards.use_when: Reviewing an AI-drafted product page, email or landing page that reads generic, and fixing it by editing the one variable that's off instead of discarding the whole draft.
steps: Identify the variables in your own writing: preferred adjectives (free vs exquisite vs a strong expletive produce completely different reads), sentence length and rhythm (long, semicolon-heavy vs short, terse, simple), and tendency toward opinion vs referenced facts.
When an AI draft doesn't sound like you, don't bin it. Locate the specific variable that's wrong.

The source's ghostwriting anecdote: a client returned a draft angry that it didn't sound like him. The only change was adding two or three references — 'according to the New York Times', 'according to Harvard Business Review' — because that client spoke in citations. He changed about one percent of the piece and the client said it sounded exactly like him.
Apply the same on your store's copy: if you write with short sentences and concrete nouns but the draft is embellished and long, compress sentences rather than rewriting the whole thing.

Recognize your own voice through small choices that come naturally: you already know which foods, which words, which rhythms you like; the source claims this is just not usually noticed until you look.
Keep a short list of your voice variables in a brand style guide so any writer or tool can match them without re-deriving them.
caveats: The source says voice is a minority component, roughly 80% of a piece being commodity word groupings with only small subjective swaps — this is his estimate from ghostwriting hundreds of clients, not a measurement.
He also reports using essentially the same authoritative voice for most clients successfully, which cuts against treating voice as fully unique.

cards.title: Write First to Discover Your Voice — Don't Wait For It
cards.summary: The source's position is that most people who say they don't like their voice are actually afraid to publish, and voice is discovered only by writing and publishing.
cards.use_when: Finding excuses to delay starting or delegating a store's content program, or when a founder says they have no voice and considers AI-generated copy a shortcut.
steps: Separate the two complaints: 'I don't know what makes my voice my voice' is a practice problem; 'I don't like putting myself out there' is a fear problem. The source argues the second is usually the real one hiding behind the first.

Get out the first draft and publish something small — a shelf-note on a product page, one story in the welcome email. Discovery of your preferred adjectives, rhythm and perspective happens through the act of writing, not before it.

Try variants deliberately: write the same paragraph in two different rhythms or two levels of formality, then judge which is yours. The source frames this as knowing whether you're a pizza or pasta person.

For a store, the operational version is writing a one-paragraph product story yourself and comparing it to what AI produces from your brief. The comparison reveals which specific variable you disagree with.

The source says people publish less than they are able to. If output is stuck, remove barriers: schedule sessions, use a template, drop your publishing volume goal — but keep the human writing step in place.
caveats: The source's 'most people are just afraid to publish' is a broad claim from a longtime ghostwriter, not a universal rule.

The same practitioner says that if you truly cannot write and know your industry, having an LLM rewrite your brain-dump as it would is no different from hiring a ghostwriter — so his standard is 'produce the raw material first,' not 'always draft it by hand.'

cards.title: Point of View Is the Moat — for a Product and a Content Program
cards.summary: SaaS and products with a specific method beat commodity feature sets because copying the output forces competitors to chase the methodology with a permanent lag.
cards.use_when: Positioning a store's product, subscription or membership, or writing the category positioning that explains why your way of doing the customer's job is different.
steps: Sharpen the store's stated point of view into one sentence — not 'sells X' but 'helps customers do X this way.' The source's example: his writing product is not a scheduling-and-writing tool (commodity), it's a tool built to help customers execute a specific method of writing online.

The source argues the moat comes from the methodology driving the feature set: someone copying a feature must first understand the terminology and reasoning behind it, putting them a step behind every time.
Write the store's content from the methodology, not just features. Every commodity idea you endorse or reject is an expression of your method.
Apply on the PDP and landing page: name the method (e.g. 'buy less, replace less often') and let product specs serve it, rather than listing specs alongside competitors.

The source's own example of how this propagates: 'commodity content, personality content, original content' — terms only covered by his own framework, requiring any copier to first reconstruct his thinking before they can publish anything comparable.
Test whether the store's point of view passes the copying test: if a competitor can hire a copywriter for a day and replicate your positioning, the 'point of view' is still a feature list.
caveats: The source's example is his own product; he is an interested party and calls the moat a claim, not a measured outcome.
It's a strong position on commoditization — the source applies it himself and to other founders, but it's not a universal law of SaaS or ecommerce.

cards.title: Use Short/Medium/Long-Term Value to Choose What to Publish
cards.summary: Ask before creating what the short-, medium- and long-term value is; the same question applied to the store's 20-minute post and its two-week essay produces very different additive contributions to the content library.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to spend content production time for a store — which single blog post, guide, or campaign gets the two-week investment versus the twenty-minute one.
steps: Before creating a piece, ask three questions: what does this get me in the next hour? In the next month? In the next years?
A 20-minute post repeating a commodity idea adds a small amount — maybe a slightly different phrasing of something you've said before, but still 'approved language' for future reuse.

A two-week essay on a topic you've never covered, where you crystallize a new point of view, adds exponentially more to the library — the source's framing is that this is what increases the value of a 'digital brain' or 'personal language model.'
The source's estimate: it took him two weeks to write one essay on AI and he expects to reference and use it for around ten years.
Apply the accounting to the store: if every content piece looks like the twenty-minute repeat, the library doesn't grow. Block time for the two-week piece.
Use the questions to justify the time investment to whoever controls the budget, and to avoid assuming every piece should return equally.
caveats: The two-week/ten-year figures are the source's personal example, not a benchmark.
The question is a planning heuristic - not a validated attribution model - so it does not replace actual measurement of content performance.

cards.title: What to Skip When Following This Framework
cards.summary: This material's useful core is the writing/publishing/ownership framework; tangential show content — sponsor reads, personal banter, agency plugs — is not part of it.
cards.use_when: Reviewing or applying the framework to decide what actually belongs in a store's content or writing-forward practice.
steps: Skip promo segments and community plugs — they don't teach the framework.

Use the underlying structure rather than the episode's packaging: the transferable components are content-value accounting, commodity vs personality vs original content, approved-language reuse, and voice as a discrete bundle of variables.

Approximately 15 percent of the source is basic definitions of content marketing and social volume; about 85 percent is the growth-level framework — this ratio is about the source, not a target for your content mix.
caveats: This card is about scope, not a procedure. Do not treat it as a step in your editorial process.
